title: Wild Atlantic Way: Dingle, Iveragh & the Burren
subRegion: County Kerry & County Clare, Wild Atlantic Way

bestPeriod.window: May–June and September for long light, open attractions and manageable traffic; July–August is peak and the coach volume on Slea Head and the Ring of Kerry is significant
bestPeriod.raw: May–June and September for long light, open attractions and manageable traffic; July–August is peak and the coach volume on Slea Head and the Ring of Kerry is significant

food.note: €55–90 per day; a seafood dinner in Dingle €40–60

transport.note: €350–500: car hire €50–80 per day plus the Irish insurance excess, fuel, one Shannon ferry

activities.note: €90–200: Skellig or Blasket boats, Cliffs of Moher, Muckross House, distillery tours

languages: Irish — the Dingle peninsula west of Dingle town is a Gaeltacht where Irish is the daily language
summary: A seven-day road trips & scenic drive itinerary in County Kerry & County Clare, Wild Atlantic Way, Ireland.

itinerary.title: Shannon or Kerry to Dingle
itinerary.morning: Land at Shannon or Kerry. Collect the car, and read the insurance excess paperwork properly before you sign — Irish CDW terms are their own genre. `verify: true`
itinerary.afternoon: Drive west to Dingle (An Daingean) via Tralee. Arrive with enough light to walk the harbour and Green Street.
itinerary.evening: Dingle is a town of about 2,000 people with an implausible density of good restaurants and pubs. Seafood dinner, then a session — traditional music happens nightly and starts around 21:30.

itinerary.title: Slea Head Drive and the Blaskets
itinerary.morning: The Slea Head Drive loop west of Dingle: beehive huts (clocháns) from the early medieval period, the Gallarus Oratory — a dry-stone corbelled chapel still watertight after twelve centuries — and Dunquin pier's zigzag ramp down the cliff.
itinerary.afternoon: In settled weather, the Blasket Islands ferry from Dunquin to Great Blasket, evacuated in 1953 and the source of an extraordinary body of Irish-language literature. Otherwise the Blasket Centre on the mainland covers it superbly.
itinerary.evening: Back to Dingle. **Driving rule:** the loop is effectively one-way by convention — go clockwise, the way the coaches go, and you will never meet one head-on in a passing place.

itinerary.title: Conor Pass and south to Portmagee
itinerary.morning: The Conor Pass — 456 m, single track in places, cut into the cliff with a lake below and a waterfall you can climb to at the top. Not for camper vans, and genuinely alarming in fog.
itinerary.afternoon: South via Inch Strand — a 5 km sand spit into Dingle Bay — then over to the Iveragh peninsula and out along the Skellig Ring to Portmagee.
itinerary.evening: Portmagee, a single row of painted houses on the harbour. The pub here is the meeting point for the Skellig boatmen; dinner and a pint is also your weather briefing.

itinerary.title: Skellig Michael or the Skellig Ring
itinerary.morning: If you have a landing permit and the sea is calm, the boat to **Skellig Michael** — a 6th-century monastery of stone beehive cells on a pyramid of rock 12 km offshore, 618 steps up, a UNESCO site with a strictly limited number of landing passes per day sold months in advance. It cancels often.
itinerary.afternoon: If not: the Skellig Ring by road — Kerry Cliffs (higher than the Cliffs of Moher and a fraction as busy), Valentia Island via the Portmagee bridge, the Geokaun mountain viewpoint, the tetrapod trackway with 385-million-year-old footprints, and the slate quarry grotto.
itinerary.evening: Portmagee or Cahersiveen. Valentia's Bray Head walk at sunset if the light holds.

itinerary.title: Ring of Kerry to Killarney
itinerary.morning: The Ring of Kerry proper: Waterville, Derrynane with its beach and O'Connell's house, and the Coomakista Pass with the whole bay beneath it.
itinerary.afternoon: Over Moll's Gap and down through Ladies View into Killarney National Park — Ireland's first, with native oakwood, red deer and the three lakes. Muckross House and the Torc Waterfall.
itinerary.evening: Killarney. Busy and unashamedly touristic, but the park at dusk is another matter entirely.

itinerary.title: Shannon ferry, Loop Head and the Cliffs of Moher
itinerary.morning: North to Tarbert and the Shannon car ferry to Killimer (20 minutes), which saves about two hours of driving around the estuary and is a pleasure in itself.
itinerary.afternoon: The Loop Head peninsula — a lighthouse, a sea arch, and almost no visitors, which is the point. Then north to the Cliffs of Moher: 14 km of cliff up to 214 m, with O'Brien's Tower and, in season, puffins on the sea stack.
itinerary.evening: Doolin. Three pubs, all with nightly traditional music, and the best trad scene per capita in Ireland.

itinerary.title: The Burren and out
itinerary.morning: The Burren: 250 km² of limestone pavement, grey and lunar, with Arctic, Alpine and Mediterranean plants growing side by side in the grikes. Poulnabrone dolmen — a portal tomb from around 3800 BC — stands alone on the rock.
itinerary.afternoon: Corkscrew Hill to Ballyvaughan, then along Galway Bay. Shannon airport is 90 minutes from Ballyvaughan; Galway city is 50 minutes north if you are continuing.

accommodationStrategy.name: Castlewood House or Pax House
accommodationStrategy.description: Two long-running guesthouses above Dingle harbour, both with sea views, serious breakfasts and hosts who will book your Blasket ferry and your dinner table. Ten minutes' walk into town, which means you can go to a session without driving.

accommodationStrategy.name: The Moorings
accommodationStrategy.description: On the harbour, above the pub, with the Skellig boat operators at the bar downstairs. If Skellig Michael is your priority, staying here is a material advantage: decisions get made at 07:30 and you will hear them first.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gregans Castle Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: A Georgian house under Corkscrew Hill looking over the Burren to Galway Bay, with one of Ireland's best restaurants and no televisions in the rooms. The right final night, and a complete change of register from the road.

logistics.emergency: 112 or 999. Coast Guard for sea and cliff incidents. Mountain rescue in Kerry via 112. University Hospital Kerry (Tralee) and University Hospital Limerick are the main facilities.
logistics.weather: Atlantic, changeable, four seasons daily. Cliff edges are unfenced in most places and grass on limestone is slippery when wet. Wind at the Cliffs of Moher regularly exceeds safe standing.
logistics.bookingWindows: June–August accommodation in Dingle, Doolin and Portmagee: 3–4 months. Gregans Castle: 3+ months. Restaurants in Dingle in summer: a week ahead, minimum.

other.label: The road is the risk
other.text: Irish regional roads (R-numbers) are posted at 80 km/h and are frequently single-track with stone walls, blind bends and no shoulder. Drive to the road, not the sign. Wing-mirror damage is the most common rental claim in Kerry and Clare.

other.label: Coach convention
other.text: Both the Ring of Kerry and Slea Head Drive are driven by tour coaches in a set direction. Follow it. Meeting a 14 m coach on a cliff-edge passing place is the trip's most avoidable stress.

other.label: Insurance
other.text: Irish car rental excess is high and third-party credit-card cover is often not accepted by Irish firms. Budget for the rental company's own super-CDW or verify your policy in writing beforehand. `verify: true`

other.label: Boats
other.text: Skellig Michael landing permits are limited by the OPW to a small daily number, sold by a handful of licensed operators, released months ahead and cancelled in swell. Book early and hold a plan B. Blasket ferries are less constrained but equally weather-dependent. `verify: true`

other.label: Fuel and cash
other.text: Fuel is available in every town; some rural pumps close at 20:00. Cards are near-universal but a few small ferries and honesty car parks want coins.

proTips: Drive the **Cliffs of Moher at 08:00 or after 18:00**. The visitor centre car park is the bottleneck; the site is open outside centre hours at reduced rates and the light is far better at both ends. `verify: true`
**Kerry Cliffs** are taller than Moher, cost a few euro to a farmer at a gate, and have perhaps a tenth of the people.
Take the **Tarbert–Killimer ferry** even if the timing is neutral. It replaces 90 minutes of estuary driving with a 20-minute crossing and a coffee.
Music sessions are not scheduled entertainment. They start when the musicians arrive, usually 21:30–22:00, and the good ones are in the pub without a sign advertising music.
The Burren is a **spring destination**: May is when the gentians, orchids and mountain avens flower on the limestone, and it is the strangest botanical sight in Europe.

If Skellig Michael cancels — and it cancels roughly one day in three — the eco-tour that circles the rock without landing still gets you the gannet colony on Little Skellig, 70,000 pairs of them, and it sails in conditions when landings cannot.

raw.driving_character: Narrow regional roads with stone walls and no shoulder; coach traffic on the two famous loops; average speeds far below posted limits
raw.mountain_passes: Conor Pass (456 m, Ireland's highest surfaced pass, unsuitable for large vehicles), Moll's Gap, Corkscrew Hill in the Burren
raw.cross_border_rules: Crossing into Northern Ireland (UK) is permitted by most Irish rental firms but requires declared cross-border cover — check before you drive north
